patient.chief_complaint: Grade 4 hepatic encephalopathy — binge alcohol relapse as precipitant
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. K. is a 48-year-old man with severe alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD 24) and a prior HE episode 3 months ago who was found unresponsive in his apartment by a neighbor. Emergency services report empty vodka bottles at the scene and the neighbor states the patient was found minimally responsive, unable to communicate. He had claimed sobriety since his outpatient detox 6 months ago. On arrival to the emergency department he has a GCS of 8 — eyes open only to pain, incomprehensible sounds, and localizing to pain. He is profoundly icteric with massive tense ascites and fetor hepaticus. Blood pressure is 108/66 with tachycardia 104. Serum ethanol is 182 mg/dL on admission, confirming active heavy alcohol use. However, the degree of encephalopathy (GCS 8) is disproportionate to the alcohol level — at 182 mg/dL, an alcohol-tolerant individual with chronic heavy use would typically be moderately intoxicated, not deeply encephalopathic. The markedly elevated ammonia of 212 µmol/L — the highest of his presentations — explains the severity of encephalopathy. The precipitants are: (1) acute heavy alcohol intake directly suppresses hepatic urea cycle enzymes and causes acute hepatic injury on top of cirrhosis; (2) binge drinking causes dehydration and electrolyte depletion that worsen HE; (3) medication non-adherence during binge (lactulose and rifaximin likely not taken). This is grade 4 HE — the most severe clinical presentation requiring ICU monitoring and airway assessment.

output.impression: Mild alcohol withdrawal — symptom-triggered benzodiazepine protocol (lorazepam 1-2 mg PRN for CIWA ≥10 or seizure). NOTE: Benzodiazepines contraindicated in severe HE (worsen encephalopathy) — use minimum effective dose only if withdrawal seizure risk is high. Phenobarbital is an alternative in refractory alcohol withdrawal with liver disease.

critical_actions: IV thiamine 500 mg BEFORE dextrose — thiamine 22 nmol/L is critical deficiency in alcoholic with hypoglycemia
Correct hypoglycemia — glucose 58 directly impairs consciousness and mimics/worsens HE
CT head urgently — thrombocytopenia 48 + INR 3.4 + unwitnessed fall — subdural hematoma risk
Lactulose via NG tube if patient cannot swallow — do not withhold lactulose in grade 4 HE
CIWA-Ar monitoring — distinguish HE from alcohol withdrawal (overlap can be fatal if withdrawal seizures occur)
Airway assessment — GCS 8 requires close monitoring for intubation threshold
Addiction medicine and transplant evaluation — MELD 24 + recurrent HE despite active drinking
contraindicated_actions: Give dextrose before thiamine: Precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy in thiamine-deficient alcoholic — thiamine first, always
Empiric benzodiazepines for presumed alcohol withdrawal: Benzodiazepines worsen hepatic encephalopathy — use CIWA-Ar guided therapy only; minimum effective dose
Avoid lactulose due to aspiration risk in low-GCS patient: Administer via NG tube or rectal route — do not withhold; lactulose is essential for ammonia reduction
Assume HE alone explains GCS 8 without CT head: Thrombocytopenia 48 and INR 3.4 with unwitnessed fall create high bleeding risk — CT head mandatory to exclude subdural
teaching_pearls: Disproportionate GCS depression to alcohol level in a cirrhotic always means elevated ammonia — do not attribute grade 4 encephalopathy to ethanol alone
Thiamine 22 nmol/L = critical deficiency — IV thiamine 500 mg TID is the correct dose (not 100 mg daily)
In grade 4 HE with GCS 8 and inability to swallow, lactulose must be given via NG tube — do not withhold because of dysphagia
CIWA-Ar helps distinguish alcohol withdrawal (peaks 48-72h after last drink) from HE — different treatment pathways
Thrombocytopenia in cirrhotics with unwitnessed episodes requires CT head to exclude subdural hematoma even when HE is the likely cause
key_reasoning_points: Alcohol level 182 mg/dL in a chronic heavy drinker does not alone explain GCS 8 — the ammonia 212 is the key contributor explaining the severity of encephalopathy; disproportionate depression of consciousness to alcohol level is a red flag
Grade 4 HE with burst suppression on EEG indicates the most severe metabolic depression — ICU monitoring required, airway at risk
Thiamine before dextrose is inviolable in alcoholic encephalopathy — level 22 nmol/L confirms high Wernicke risk

Benzodiazepine-alcohol withdrawal overlap with HE creates a clinical dilemma: CIWA-Ar guides the minimum necessary benzodiazepine dose; phenobarbital is preferable if large benzodiazepine doses are needed
Active alcohol use complicates transplant candidacy — most centers require 6 months sobriety, but early consultation with addiction medicine is essential regardless
